h1:
Thong Sala Night Market
Koh Phangan: What to Eat
intro: If you come to Koh Phangan and want to eat your fill at local prices rather than beachfront markups, Thong Sala Night Market — which everyone on the island just calls Phantip Market — is the first place to head. It sits right in Thong Sala town near the pier, opens every day, and gathers Thai street food, punchy Southern dishes, charcoal grills and homestyle desserts in one spot. We've eaten our way through it and picked out which plates are worth trying, roughly what they cost, and when the crowds are thinner.

blocks.html: Phantip Market sits in the middle of Thong Sala town on the island's southwest side, just a few minutes' walk from Thong Sala Pier. The big draw is that it opens every single day, so it's the safest bet no matter which night you land on the island. The market splits into two parts: shops in the buildings around the edge, and open-air stalls in the central yard. The open-air section is the real star for food lovers — grills, fried snacks, made-to-order dishes and desserts all cluster close together, so one loop shows you everything.

Prices here are friendly compared with the beachfront spots over at Haad Rin. Most main Thai dishes run about ฿50–100, grilled skewers are a handful of baht each, and desserts start at just ฿5–20. Western food like pizza, sushi or Indian curry climbs higher, to ฿150–250 depending on ingredients. Bring enough cash, because almost all the small stalls take cash only.

blocks.text: Opening hours and when to go

items: Open daily. Stalls start setting up in the late afternoon, around 16:00–17:00, and are in full swing until about 22:00 — sometimes later on busier nights.
Peak crowds are 19:00–21:00. Come then if you want every stall open, but expect to squeeze through.
For a relaxed wander, arrive before 18:30, when the grills are fresh on the coals and it's easy to pick a stall before the rush.
On Saturdays, the main road in Thong Sala closes for a Walking Street with extra stalls and live music — a different zone from Phantip Market, but you can walk between the two in one night.

blocks.title: Carry cash
blocks.html: Almost every stall in the market is cash only. There are ATMs in Thong Sala town, but foreign-card withdrawal fees are steep, so it's best to withdraw before you head over to the island and keep small notes handy for easy change.

blocks.text: Standout plates to try, with rough prices

blocks.html: We've ordered these by how worth-it they are for a first-timer, mixing Thai-Southern savoury dishes, grills and sweets. Prices are rough ranges from actually walking the market — they may shift a bit by stall and season.

items.name: Charcoal grills — moo ping & grilled chicken
items.blurb: The grill stalls are the first smell that pulls people in. Sweet-marinated, tender pork skewers and crispy-skinned grilled chicken, eaten with hot sticky rice, make an easy, cheap, filling meal. Pick a stall grilling fresh in front of you so it comes off the coals hot.
items.price: Pork skewers ฿10–15 each · sticky rice ฿10

items.name: Fried chicken + sticky rice
items.blurb: Southern-style fried chicken with crisp skin, fried fresh by the tray so you can pick the pieces you want. Pay by the piece, eat it with sticky rice, and you're full for a few dozen baht. It's a favourite of the working locals on the island.

items.name: Southern curry over rice — gaeng leuang, moo hong
items.blurb: This is where the market's Southern soul shows. The curry-over-rice stalls let you pick from several dishes: gaeng leuang (sour-spicy yellow curry done the real Southern way) and moo hong (sweet, tender braised pork). Two scoops over rice fills you up cheaply. It's genuinely spicy if you're not used to Southern flavours — just ask the cook to ease off the chilli.

items.name: Pad Thai
items.blurb: Pad Thai with shrimp or chicken, stir-fried hot in front of you with egg and bean sprouts and a sprinkle of crushed peanuts. It's the plate everyone can eat — easy to find at several stalls, mild rather than fiery, and a safe bet if you're not ready to risk Southern heat.

items.name: Som tam — Thai-style or pla ra
items.blurb: Pounded fresh in front of you, with the spice level your call. Tam Thai is well-balanced for first-timers, while spice lovers can try the punchy pla ra (fermented fish) version. Eat it with grilled chicken and sticky rice for the classic set.

items.name: Tom yum / tom kha gai
items.blurb: A hot bowl of soup to cut the richness of all the grilled food. Tom yum goong is tangy and spicy; tom kha gai is creamy and mellow with coconut milk. Order it alongside steamed rice and it's a full meal.

items.name: Grilled seafood — prawns, squid
items.blurb: It's an island, so of course there's seafood. Grilled prawns and squid with a punchy seafood dipping sauce. Pick a stall cooking it through in front of you, and skip raw items that have been sitting out a while. Prices move with size and season, so always ask before you order.

items.name: Roti — banana, condensed milk, chocolate
items.blurb: A sweet finish that kids and adults love alike. Roti dough fried crisp outside and soft inside, with banana and a drizzle of condensed milk or chocolate, made fresh and hot. You'll find it at several stalls.

items.name: Mango sticky rice
items.blurb: The Thai dessert visitors fall for — sweet coconut sticky rice paired with ripe, juicy mango. It's seasonal, so in the hot season there's more of it and it tastes better.

items.name: Homestyle Thai sweets — khanom krok, khao tom mat
items.blurb: Little Thai-sweets stalls selling khanom krok (crisp outside, soft inside), khao tom mat and khanom thuay, all very cheap. Grab a few to nibble while you walk — easy on the wallet and a corner where locals actually stop.

items.name: Coconut rice balls
items.blurb: A sweet that travellers review often — fried dough fragrant with coconut, crisp outside and chewy inside. Buy a bag and snack as you wander; it's a treat you don't find easily elsewhere.

items.name: Fruit smoothies / Thai iced tea
items.blurb: Finish with a fresh fruit smoothie — mango, watermelon, passion fruit — or a sweet, creamy Thai iced tea, all several times cheaper than the beachfront cafes. A great way to cool off after walking the market.

blocks.title: Choose raw seafood wisely
blocks.html: Some stalls display raw seafood on ice. If you're after seafood, pick a stall that grills or cooks it through in front of you, and avoid raw items that have been sitting out in the heat for a long time. Confirm the price per kilo or per plate before you order so there are no surprises when you pay.

If you're staying in Thong Sala or nearby, splitting it across two nights lets you try everything without getting too stuffed. Night one leans savoury, night two saves desserts and seafood. Here's a rough guide.

blocks.text: Getting to the market and parking

items: The market is in the middle of Thong Sala town, about a 5–10 minute walk from Thong Sala Pier — handy if you arrive by ferry, which lands right here.
Riding your own motorbike is the easiest option, with roadside parking around the market — though the town roads get busy in the evening, so ride slowly.
If you're staying at another beach like Haad Rin or the north, you can take a songthaew (local taxi) in. Always agree the price before you get on.
Many stretches of road on the island are steep and slippery, especially after rain. If you ride a motorbike yourself you need a licence, wear a helmet, and take care on the downhill sections.

blocks.title: Ride safely on the island
blocks.html: Motorbike accidents are common on Koh Phangan — the roads are steep and the sand makes them slippery. If you're not used to riding on hills, don't push it: a songthaew or a driver pick-up is safer. And on a night when you've been drinking, never ride yourself.

blocks.text: Eating at the market on Full Moon night

blocks.html: Koh Phangan is famous for the Full Moon Party at Haad Rin, and on party nights the whole island gets far more crowded, with Thong Sala market busier than usual too. If you want to eat before heading to the party, come early in the evening and then make your way to Haad Rin, because late at night the traffic jams up and songthaew prices go up.

items: Drink sensibly — know your limit, don't accept drinks from strangers, and don't leave your glass unattended.
Watch your valuables — carry only what you need and keep your phone and wallet tucked away; things go missing easily in big crowds.
Water safety — don't swim while drunk or late at night; the night-time currents are dangerous.
Room prices swing hard — on nights near the full moon, room rates spike and fill fast, and many places enforce multi-night minimum stays, so plan and book ahead.

faq.q: What days is Thong Sala Night Market (Phantip Market) open?
faq.a: It's open every day. Stalls start opening in the late afternoon, around 16:00–17:00, and stay busy until about 22:00, sometimes later. The busiest stretch is 19:00–21:00, and on Saturdays there's an added Thong Sala Walking Street along the main road.

faq.q: What should I eat at Phantip Market?
faq.a: Charcoal grills like moo ping and grilled chicken with sticky rice make a cheap, filling meal. If you want to try Southern flavours, go for gaeng leuang curry over rice or moo hong. The most popular desserts are roti, coconut rice balls, and mango sticky rice when it's in season.

faq.q: Is the food at Thong Sala market expensive?
faq.a: It's friendly compared with the beachfront spots. Main Thai dishes run about ฿50–100, grilled skewers are a handful of baht each, and desserts start at ฿5–20. Western food like pizza, sushi or Indian curry climbs up to ฿150–250.

faq.q: Does the market take cards or do I need cash?
faq.a: Almost all the small stalls are cash only. It's best to withdraw cash before you head to the island and keep small notes for easy change. There are ATMs in town, but foreign-card fees are steep.

faq.q: How do I get to Thong Sala market from the pier?
faq.a: The market is in the middle of Thong Sala town, about a 5–10 minute walk from Thong Sala Pier. If you're staying at another beach you can take a songthaew in — agree the price first — or ride your own motorbike, with roadside parking around the market.
